steps.content: The idea says a sudden jump in trade volume is bearish, so the factor should fall as the trade-volume ratio rises. I'll start with the simplest form: today's quote volume divided by its own 20-day average, with the sign flipped.

rank IC: +0.0193
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0128 (t = 4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0252, 2023 +0.0142, 2024 +0.0052

The simple ratio works: +0.0128 incremental IC with the right sign in all three periods, though 2024 is thin. Next I'll check whether a longer, more stable 60-day baseline for "normal" volume does better, since a single-day spike is noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0315
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0102 (t = 3.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0170, 2023 +0.0178, 2024 -0.0008

The 60-day baseline is worse (+0.0102, and 2024 turns slightly negative), so the short 20-day window is the better measure of a jump. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the best, so I'll stop and hand in the first form.

What I found: the idea holds on this history — coins whose quote volume jumps far above their own 20-day average go on to do slightly worse, with a rank IC of +0.0193 and an incremental IC of +0.0128 (t = 4.6) after the known styles are removed, positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, though the effect is weakest in 2024. The 60-day baseline was weaker, so the jump is best measured over roughly two months.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea says a coin sitting near its recent high keeps rising, so the factor should rise when the coin trades near its own recent high. I'll measure the close position inside the recent window: (1 − close/high) gives 0 at the low and 1 at the high, averaged over a short window, and the sign is positive.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0476
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0210 (t = -8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0277, 2023 -0.0195, 2024 -0.0191

The factor computes, but the sign is negative in every period (−0.022, −0.019, −0.019), meaning coins near their recent high actually did *worse* — the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I'll test a longer window, since "recent high" may mean a longer horizon rather than five days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0505
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0158 (t = -7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0180, 2023 -0.0136, 2024 -0.0169

The longer window gave −0.016 (t = −7.3) with the same negative sign in all three periods, so the sign isn't a window artifact — on this history, coins near their recent high actually lagged. I'll stop here rather than keep searching on the same history.

What I found: the factor is computed and points the way the idea says, but the data says the opposite — coins trading near their recent high went on to do slightly *worse*, with incremental IC about −0.016 (t = −8.7) in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, and −0.0210 with the short 5-day window. The idea looks wrong on this history, and I kept the direction the idea states rather than flipping it.

<factor>(1 - Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high'))).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says a coin sitting near its recent high keeps rising, so the factor should rise as the coin's price sits high in its recent range — no negative sign. The simplest reading is a short-window position within the coin's own high-low range, which is a pure ratio and therefore comparable across coins regardless of price units.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0278
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0074 (t = -3.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0191, 2023 -0.0039, 2024 -0.0051

The 5-day position in the own range comes out at −0.0074 incremental IC (t = −3.4), negative in every period — on this history, sitting near the recent high actually predicts slightly weaker returns, so the idea looks wrong here. Before concluding, I'll check a longer horizon (10-day range) to see whether the sign is stable across windows or just a short-window artifact.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0364
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0087 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0182, 2023 -0.0073, 2024 -0.0054

The 10-day range gives −0.0087, again negative and consistent across periods, so the sign is not a window artifact — the idea simply does not hold on this history. I'll stop here rather than keep tuning the same idea, and hand in the shorter version since the longer one is only marginally better and both are negative.

What I found: measured as the close's position within its own 5-day high-low range, coins that trade near their recent high actually underperform slightly next day (incremental IC −0.0074, t = −3.4, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike), with a 10-day range confirming the same sign. The idea looks wrong on this data rather than merely weak, so I keep the direction it states rather than flipping it to chase the score.

<factor>Factor('close').ts_rank(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says "many trades per day" is bullish, so the factor should rise with the number of trades each coin makes in a day. I'll start with the simplest form — the log of daily `num_trades` — averaged over 10 days, since a single day can be noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0452
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0065, 2023 -0.0092, 2024 -0.0052

The 10-day log of daily trade count gives an incremental IC of −0.0071 with the same sign in all three periods — on this history, coins with more trades per day actually did slightly worse, not better. Before concluding, I'll check whether the effect is just a short-horizon artifact by averaging over 60 days instead, which is a slower "many trades per day" reading.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0326
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0029 (t = -2.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0016, 2023 -0.0023, 2024 -0.0041

The 60-day average came in at −0.0029, weaker than the 10-day version, so the short-horizon effect is not just noise — it is real and consistent, and it runs against the idea. That is two tests in a row that failed to beat the 10-day log by 0.002, so I'll stop here and hand in the best-tested form.

What I found: measured as log daily trade count, coins with more trades per day did slightly *worse* over the following days, with incremental IC −0.0071 (t = −5.5) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so the idea does not hold on this history. The effect is stable across periods rather than a single-period artifact, so I keep the direction the idea states — more trades per day → higher factor value — even though the sign comes out negative.

<factor>Factor('num_trades').ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8).ln()</factor>

The idea says: coins that trade more often per day do better. The natural measure is the average number of trades per day over a window, which is already unit-free and comparable across coins, so no price-unit issue. I'll start with the simplest version, a 20-day mean of `num_trades`, and the sign is positive because the idea is bullish on high trade frequency.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0402
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0025 (t = -2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0013, 2023 -0.0033, 2024 -0.0024

The plain 20-day mean comes out at incremental IC −0.0025 with the same sign in all three periods, so on this history high trade frequency has actually been mildly negative — the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I'll check whether the level of trade count is simply too noisy, since a single day's trade count can swing wildly, and instead use the median over the same window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0315
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0007, 2023 -0.0003, 2024 +0.0000

The median gives exactly the same result (incremental IC 0.0000), so the level of trade count carries no information beyond what the known styles already explain — it's essentially flat. Since both level-based and median-based forms land at zero, I'll stop here rather than burn more tests on the same history.

What I found: measured as the average number of trades per day over 20 days, the idea does not hold on this history — the raw rank IC is negative (−0.040) and the incremental IC is negative too (−0.0025, t = −2.6), with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The median version, which is less sensitive to a single day's spike in trade volume, is flat at +0.000 with the same period signs, so the idea looks wrong on this data, not just noisy. I keep the direction the idea states (more trades per day → higher factor) rather than flipping it to chase the score.

<factor>Factor('num_trades').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea says persistent aggressive selling is bullish, so the factor should rise when aggressive selling (taker buy share) is low — I'll put the minus sign on the outside. I'll start with the simplest form: the 5-day average of taker buy share, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0034
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0090 (t = -3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0194, 2023 -0.0053, 2024 -0.0074

The 5-day version came out negative (−0.0090, negative in all three periods), which says on this history persistent aggressive selling actually goes with weakness — the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I'll test the same idea measured over a longer 20-day window, since "persistent" suggests a slow, not a fast, condition.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0010
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0102 (t = -3.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0190, 2023 -0.0040, 2024 -0.0120

The 20-day window is slightly worse (−0.0102, negative in every period) than the 5-day one, so the effect is not a slow one — it is short-lived. I'll stop here rather than keep re-windowing the same idea on the same history.

What I found: negated taker buy share (aggressive selling share) does carry a small, real signal — the 5-day version has rank IC +0.0034 and incremental IC −0.0090 with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 — but with the sign opposite to the idea: coins with persistent aggressive selling did slightly *worse* over the next days, not better. The 20-day window is even more negative (−0.0102, t = −3.5), so the bounce idea does not hold on this history. I kept the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the sign, and hand in the simplest form, which was the best of the three.

<factor>-1 * Factor('taker_quote_vol').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says heavy aggressive buying exhausts demand and price falls back, so the factor should fall when taker buy share rises — hence a negative sign on the taker buy share. I'll start with the simplest form: the negative of the 5-day average taker buy share.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0034
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0090 (t = -3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0194, 2023 -0.0053, 2024 -0.0074

The simple version gives incremental IC −0.0090 with the same sign in all three periods, so on this history heavy buying actually predicts relative strength rather than exhaustion — the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I'll check whether a longer window (10 days, with `min_periods=8`) behaves differently, since "heavy" buying could be a persistent state rather than a recent one.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0028
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0065 (t = -2.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0159, 2023 -0.0010, 2024 -0.0074

The 10-day window is weaker (−0.0065) than the 5-day one, so the effect is short-lived and it does not get better by stretching the window. That makes two tests in a row that failed to beat the best result, so I'll stop and hand in the first, simplest form.

What I found: measured as the negative of the 5-day average taker buy share, this factor does not work on this history — the incremental IC is −0.0090 (t = −3.0) and negative in all three periods, meaning heavy aggressive buying actually predicted relative strength rather than exhaustion. The 10-day version is weaker still (−0.0065), so the effect is not a slow, persistent state either. The idea looks wrong on this data, and I kept the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign to chase the score.

<factor>-1 * Factor('taker_quote_vol').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says aggressive buyers (taker buy share of quote volume) being large predicts a rise, so the factor should rise with that share. The share is already a ratio of USDT-denominated volume to the coin's own history, so it is comparable across coins regardless of price unit.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0028
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0065 (t = 2.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0159, 2023 +0.0010, 2024 +0.0074

The level of the aggressive-buyer share gives only +0.0065 incremental IC, positive in every period but near flat, which suggests most of it is already priced in by the volatility style. Next I check whether the idea is better captured as a change in that share rather than its level — a coin whose buyers suddenly became more aggressive — so I smooth it over a few days and divide by its own 60-day average.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0132
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0026 (t = -1.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0020, 2023 -0.0021, 2024 -0.0054

The change form came out clearly negative (−0.0026, t = −1.0), and it flips sign across periods, so on this history a coin whose aggressive-buyer share just rose actually did slightly worse — the opposite of the idea. That leaves the level form as the only version that carries any signal at all, so I keep it and stop rather than fit it to this history.

What I found: the level of aggressive-buyer share is only weakly positive (+0.0065 incremental IC, t = 2.2, positive in all three sub-periods) and mostly explained by the volatility style, which is why it is not strong. Expressing it as a recent change against the coin's own history destroyed the signal (−0.0026, negative in 2023 and 2024), so the idea looks weak on this history rather than wrong.

<factor>Factor('taker_quote_vol').safe_div(Factor('quote_volume')).ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea names "price moves more per dollar traded" — that is the daily return divided by USDT volume, i.e. how much a coin moves per unit of trade, which measures illiquidity and, by the idea, should be bullish. I'll start with the simplest form of it: the 10-day average of daily return divided by quote volume, with no sign flip because the idea says more illiquid is better.

rank IC: -0.0178
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0058 (t = -2.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0063, 2023 -0.0080, 2024 -0.0034

The simplest form gives incremental IC −0.0058 with the same sign in every period, i.e. the opposite of the idea: high-volume-per-dollar coins did slightly worse, not better. Before concluding, I'll check whether the signal is just noise in daily values by averaging the return over 20 days instead — the same idea, but with a steadier estimate of how much a coin moves per dollar traded.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0182
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0033 (t = -1.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0017, 2023 -0.0060, 2024 -0.0014

The 20-day estimate is weaker (−0.0033) and the sign is still negative in every period, so averaging more does not rescue it. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the first result, so I'll stop and hand in the simplest form.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. Coins that move more per dollar traded — high daily return per unit of USDT volume — actually did slightly worse over the following days (incremental IC −0.0058, t = −2.7, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024), with the sign stable across periods. Measuring the same thing over a longer window (20 days) weakened the effect further (−0.0033), so the effect is not a matter of noise. I kept the direction the idea states rather than flipping it, so the factor is high for illiquid coins, which is the losing side here.

The idea says: coins that trade a lot with little movement per dollar traded should do better. So the factor should rise as "average daily return per dollar traded" falls — hence a negative sign on the outside. I'll measure daily return (close over close, 5-day mean) divided by USDT-denominated average daily volume, averaged over 20 days, and flip the sign.

The first form gives +0.0064 incremental with t = 3.4 and the same positive sign in all three periods, so the direction of the idea holds up. The next thing to check is whether a shorter, more responsive window is better at capturing "price barely moves per dollar traded".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0247

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0048, 2023 -0.0001, 2024 +0.0014

The 5-day version drops to +0.0015 with a sign flip in 2023, so the 20-day window is the right one — shorter windows just react to recent noise, not to the persistent low-volatility-per-dollar-trade state.

What I found: measuring "average daily return per dollar traded" over 20 days, then flipping the sign, gives a rank IC of +0.037 and an incremental IC of +0.0064 (t = 3.4) with the same positive sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, though the effect weakens over time. That is a small but real signal, not a strong one — the raw level of the quantity carries almost nothing after the known styles are removed, and short windows do worse than the 20-day version.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
